framework: CIS AWS Foundations v1.5.0 + AWS Security Best Practices
description: Comprehensive Identity and Access Management (IAM) security checks

items.title: Root account must have MFA enabled
items.description: MFA on root account prevents unauthorized access even if root credentials are compromised. Root has no limits on actions.
items.remediation: Enable MFA on root account via AWS Console → Account Settings → Multi-factor Authentication

pci_dss.reason: This control requires MFA for all non-console administrative access into the Cardholder Data Environment (CDE). The root user is the highest privileged account, and enabling MFA is a direct implementation of this requirement to protect it.

This control demands access to be based on job classification and function, following the principle of least privilege. Securing the root account with MFA ensures that only the true owner can perform the unrestricted actions associated with this unique, highly-privileged role.

items.title: IAM users should have MFA enabled (especially privileged users)
items.description: MFA provides additional layer of security. Critical for users with administrative or console access permissions.
items.remediation: Enable MFA for each IAM user with console access. Enforce via policies if needed.

pci_dss.reason: This control requires MFA for all access into the CDE. Enforcing MFA for all IAM users, especially those with access to the CDE, directly meets this requirement.

This control specifies that MFA must use at least two different factor types and that success of all is required for access. Enabling MFA for IAM users is the first step in implementing a compliant MFA system.

items.title: Remove unused IAM credentials (>90 days inactive)
items.description: Inactive credentials increase attack surface. Remove or rotate credentials that haven't been used in 90+ days.
items.remediation: Remove inactive access keys. For users still needed, force rotation via rotation policy.

pci_dss.reason: This control requires that inactive user accounts are removed or disabled within 90 days. This IAM check directly enforces this rule for credentials, reducing the risk of dormant accounts being compromised.

items.title: Access keys should be rotated every 90 days
items.description: Regular rotation reduces impact of compromised credentials. AWS recommends 90-day rotation.
items.remediation: Implement automated key rotation. Create new key → Update applications → Delete old key after verification.

pci_dss.reason: This control requires changing passwords/passphrases at least every 90 days for single-factor authentication. While access keys are not passwords, they are authentication factors, and rotating them every 90 days applies the same security principle to programmatic access.

items.title: IAM password policy minimum length should be 14+ characters
items.description: Longer passwords reduce brute-force attack risk. 14+ chars recommended.
items.remediation: Set: aws iam update-account-password-policy --minimum-password-length 14

pci_dss.reason: This control requires passwords/passphrases to have a minimum length of 12 characters. Enforcing a length of 14+ characters exceeds this minimum requirement, strengthening security against brute-force attacks.

items.title: IAM password policy should prevent password reuse
items.description: Prevents users from reusing old passwords. Should remember at least 24 previous passwords.
items.remediation: Set: aws iam update-account-password-policy --password-reuse-prevention 24

pci_dss.reason: This control mandates that new passwords/passphrases cannot be the same as the four previously used ones. Configuring a reuse prevention of 24 significantly exceeds this requirement, enhancing password history protection.

items.title: Inline policies must not be used. Use managed policies instead
items.description: Managed policies provide version control, reusability, and easier delegation. Inline policies are deprecated.
items.remediation: Migrate inline policies to managed policies using CloudFormation or AWS CLI.

pci_dss.reason: This control requires assigning access based on job classification and least privilege. Managed policies facilitate this by creating reusable sets of permissions for specific job functions, making access control more standardized, auditable, and less prone to error than managing numerous inline policies.

items.title: No policy should have full administrative permissions (*:*)
items.description: Policies granting all actions on all resources violate principle of least privilege.
items.remediation: Review policies. Replace broad permissions with specific actions and resources.

pci_dss.reason: This is a direct implementation of the principle of 'least privileges required to perform a job function.' A policy with '*:*' grants maximum privilege, which is the opposite of the least privilege principle mandated by this control.

This control requires access control systems to be set to 'deny all' by default. Granting '*:*' permissions effectively sets the default to 'allow all', directly contravening this foundational security principle.

items.title: Root account should not have active access keys
items.description: Root account with access keys provides programmatic access with unlimited permissions. Highest risk.
items.remediation: Delete root access keys: aws iam delete-access-key --access-key-id KEY_ID (requires root login)

pci_dss.reason: This control requires managing vendor default accounts, including changing passwords or disabling them if not used. The root account is the ultimate 'default' account, and disabling its programmatic access keys is a critical hardening step.

The root account should not be used for daily operational tasks. Prohibiting access keys for the root account enforces the principle of least privilege by forcing the use of IAM roles and users with specific, limited permissions for programmatic access.

items.title: Administrative users must have MFA enabled
items.description: Users with AdministratorAccess or similar elevated permissions without MFA pose critical risk.
items.remediation: Enforce MFA requirement for admin users via deny policy for non-MFA actions.

pci_dss.reason: This is a direct mapping. The control requires MFA for all non-console administrative access into the CDE. This IAM check ensures that AWS administrators, who have privileged access, are protected by MFA.

items.title: IAM role trust policies should not allow public access (*)
items.description: Trust policies with Principal: '*' allow any AWS account to assume the role. Severely restricted.
items.remediation: Update trust policy to restrict to specific AWS accounts/services. Use ExternalId for cross-account.

pci_dss.reason: This control requires that access is based on need-to-know. A trust policy allowing public access ('*') violates this by definition, as it permits access from any principal, not just those with a legitimate business need.

This control requires restricting inbound traffic to only what is necessary and denying all other traffic. A public IAM role is analogous to an open door in the firewall, allowing unnecessary and untrusted access into the environment.

items.title: Inactive users (no login in 90+ days) should be removed or disabled
items.description: Users not accessing the system for 90+ days represent unnecessary attack surface.
items.remediation: Review credential report. Disable inactive users: aws iam delete-login-profile --user-name USER

pci_dss.reason: This control explicitly requires that inactive user accounts are removed or disabled within 90 days. This IAM check is a direct implementation of that requirement.

items.title: Access keys should never be left unused (>30 days) but active
items.description: Active but unused keys suggest zombie accounts or compromised credentials not in use.
items.remediation: Review unused keys. Either delete if not needed or rotate if in use. Set reminder for regular audits.

pci_dss.reason: This control requires a review of all user accounts and privileges at least every six months to ensure access remains appropriate. Identifying and removing unused but active keys is a critical part of this access review process to reduce the attack surface.

While this control specifies 90 days for user accounts, the principle of removing inactive credentials applies. Unused keys represent a form of inactive account that should be disabled or removed to prevent potential misuse.

items.title: Users should not have multiple active access keys (except during rotation)
items.description: Multiple active keys per user increases credential compromise risk and complicates key management.
items.remediation: Review users with multiple keys. Delete old keys after confirming new ones work in all systems.

pci_dss.reason: This control requires that all users are assigned a unique ID. While multiple keys are tied to one user ID, minimizing the number of active credentials per user simplifies auditing and strengthens the association between an action and a specific credential, supporting the goal of unique identification.

items.title: Users should not have direct permissions (use groups instead)
items.description: Direct user permissions bypass group-level management, making auditing and updates difficult.
items.remediation: Create groups by function/role. Move permissions to groups. Remove direct user permissions.

pci_dss.reason: This control requires that access is based on user's job classification and functions. Using groups is the standard mechanism to implement role-based access control (RBAC). Assigning permissions to groups instead of individual users ensures that access is consistently applied based on role.

pci_dss.description: This control requires the access control system to enforce permissions based on job classification. Group-based permissions are the technical enforcement of this policy, making the system more manageable and auditable.

items.title: Service accounts should use roles, not IAM users
items.description: Service accounts (only access keys, no password) should be replaced with roles for better auditability.
items.remediation: Migrate to IAM roles with STS AssumeRole for service-to-service authentication.

pci_dss.reason: This control specifies how application and system accounts should be managed, including assigning least privilege. IAM roles are the preferred AWS mechanism for this, as they provide temporary, automatically-rotated credentials, which is far more secure than using static, long-lived access keys associated with an IAM user.

This control governs the interactive use of application and system accounts. While roles are typically for programmatic access, replacing user-based service accounts with roles helps prevent their misuse for interactive logins and ensures their privileges are strictly for application needs.

items.title: Cross-account access must include ExternalId for security
items.description: Cross-account roles without ExternalId can be assumed by other accounts without additional verification.
items.remediation: Add ExternalId condition to trust policy: 'sts:ExternalId': 'unique-external-id'

pci_dss.reason: This control requires MFA systems to not be susceptible to replay attacks or bypass. The ExternalId is a crucial defense against the 'confused deputy' problem in cross-account access, which is a form of bypass. It ensures that only the intended third party in a specific context can assume the role.

This control requires that access is based on need-to-know. Using an ExternalId ensures that cross-account role assumption is more specific and secure, preventing unauthorized principals within the trusted account from gaining access.

items.title: IAM password policy should enforce maximum password age
items.description: Users should be forced to change passwords periodically (90 days recommended).
items.remediation: Set: aws iam update-account-password-policy --max-password-age 90

pci_dss.reason: This control explicitly requires that passwords/passphrases are changed at least once every 90 days for single-factor authentication implementations. Setting a maximum password age directly enforces this requirement.

items.title: IAM password policy should require symbol characters
items.description: Password complexity improves resistance to brute-force attacks. Symbols add entropy.
items.remediation: Set: aws iam update-account-password-policy --require-symbols

pci_dss.reason: This control mandates password complexity, including the use of both numeric and alphabetic characters. While symbols are not explicitly required by the base control, they are a recommended industry best practice for strong passwords and significantly enhance password complexity, aligning with the spirit of the requirement.

items.title: Users should not exist without group assignment
items.description: Users in groups enable centralized permission management and policy enforcement.
items.remediation: Review users. Assign each user to appropriate functional group (Developers, Admins, etc.)

pci_dss.reason: This control mandates access based on job classification. A user without a group assignment likely has no defined role or has permissions attached directly, making it difficult to audit and manage access based on their function. Ensuring all users are in groups helps enforce this.

items.title: Empty groups should be removed
items.description: Groups with no members add maintenance burden and create confusion about organizational structure.
items.remediation: Delete empty groups: aws iam delete-group --group-name GROUP_NAME (after removing any policies)

pci_dss.reason: This control requires maintaining an accurate inventory of in-scope system components. While an IAM group is not a server, it is a component of the access control system. Removing empty, unused groups simplifies the environment and contributes to a cleaner, more accurate, and less confusing inventory of access control elements.

items.title: Roles unused for 90+ days should be reviewed for removal
items.description: Unused roles represent technical debt and potential security blind spots.
items.remediation: Use AWS Access Analyzer to identify unused roles. Delete or archive after confirmation.

pci_dss.reason: This control requires a review of all user accounts and privileges at least every six months. Roles are a form of account with privileges, and reviewing them for inactivity is a key part of ensuring access remains appropriate and necessary.

This control requires removing or disabling inactive user accounts within 90 days. The same principle applies to roles; an unused role is an inactive identity that increases the attack surface and should be removed.

items.title: CloudTrail should log IAM API events
items.description: Logging IAM events enables detection of unauthorized access attempts and configuration changes.
items.remediation: Enable CloudTrail for multi-region with logging to S3: aws cloudtrail create-trail --name default --s3-bucket-name BUCKET

pci_dss.reason: This control requires audit logs to be enabled and active for all system components. AWS CloudTrail is the service that generates audit logs. Ensuring it is active is fundamental to meeting this requirement.
This control requires logging all actions taken by any individual with administrative access. IAM events logged by CloudTrail provide a detailed record of these actions.
This control requires that changes to identification and authentication credentials (like creating accounts or elevating privileges) are logged. IAM API events are precisely these types of changes.

items.title: IAM Access Analyzer should be enabled
items.description: Access Analyzer identifies resources shared with external principals and validates against policies.
items.remediation: Enable: aws accessanalyzer create-analyzer --analyzer-name ConsoleAnalyzer --type ACCOUNT

pci_dss.reason: This control requires a periodic review of user accounts and privileges. Access Analyzer automates a critical part of this review by continuously monitoring and reporting on which resources are accessible to external principals, helping to ensure access remains appropriate.

items.title: Customer-managed IAM policies should not duplicate AWS managed policies
items.description: Redundant policies create maintenance overhead and inconsistency. Use AWS managed policies when possible.
items.remediation: Compare custom policies with AWS managed policies. Consolidate and remove duplicates.

pci_dss.reason: This control requires a formal change control process. Simplifying the policy landscape by using standard, managed policies where possible makes the security impact analysis for any change much easier and more reliable.

items.title: Permission boundaries should be used for delegated administration
items.description: Permission boundaries limit maximum permissions for delegated roles, adding security layer.
items.remediation: Define permission boundary policies. Apply to delegated admin roles.

pci_dss.reason: This control requires implementing access control based on least privilege. A permissions boundary is a technical enforcement mechanism that sets the maximum permissions an identity can have, preventing privilege escalation even if its own policies are overly permissive. This is a powerful tool for enforcing least privilege for delegated administrators.

This control mandates that privileges assigned are based on job classification. Permission boundaries help enforce this by ensuring that even if a delegated admin tries to grant themselves more power, they cannot exceed the 'boundary' set for their job function.

items.title: IAM account alias should be configured for console access
items.description: Alias makes console login more user-friendly and branded. Currently may use account number.
items.remediation: Create alias: aws iam create-account-alias --account-alias my-company-name

pci_dss.reason: This check has a weak but plausible link to security. The control requires that information security roles and responsibilities are clearly defined. An account alias makes the login URL clearer and more recognizable (e.g., 'my-company.signin.aws.amazon.com'), which can help prevent users from accidentally logging into the wrong account or being phished with a fake URL that uses the account number.

items.title: Tags should be consistently applied to IAM resources
items.description: Tags enable cost allocation, automation, and better resource organization.
items.remediation: Tag resources for Environment, Owner, Application, CostCenter: aws iam tag-user --user-name USER --tags Key=Env,Value=prod

pci_dss.reason: This control requires maintaining an inventory of all in-scope system components. While tags are not the inventory itself, they are a critical mechanism for identifying and managing that inventory. For example, a 'pci-scope=true' tag allows for easy identification, automation, and reporting on all components relevant to the CDE.

items.title: Detect privilege escalation via AssumeRole chains
items.description: Role trust chains that allow broad or wildcard principals can enable escalation from low-privilege identities to highly privileged roles.
items.remediation: Restrict trust policies to specific principals, require ExternalId where applicable, and add MFA conditions for privileged role assumption.

pci_dss.reason: Least-privilege access must be enforced; unrestricted trust chains violate access boundary requirements.

items.title: Resource-based policies should not allow broad cross-account principals
items.description: S3/Lambda/SQS/SNS resource policies granting wildcard or broad cross-account principals increase risk of unauthorized access and abuse.
items.remediation: Constrain principals to explicit ARNs and add source/account conditions in resource-based policies.

pci_dss.reason: Access to resources must be restricted to explicitly authorized principals.

items.title: Instance profiles should avoid over-privileged role permissions
items.description: Over-privileged roles attached to EC2 instance profiles can be abused via metadata credential theft and lateral movement.
items.remediation: Reduce instance-profile role privileges, remove admin-equivalent actions, and isolate high-risk permissions behind scoped roles.

pci_dss.reason: Compute identities must operate with least privilege to reduce blast radius if compromised.

items.title: OIDC role trust policies (GitHub Actions) must be tightly scoped
items.description: Roles trusting token.actions.githubusercontent.com without strict subject/audience conditions can be assumed by unintended GitHub workflows.
items.remediation: Require strict Conditions for GitHub OIDC trust: aud=sts.amazonaws.com and sub pinned to exact org/repo/branch/environment (avoid broad wildcards).

pci_dss.reason: Federated role assumption must be limited to explicit workload identities following least privilege.

items.title: Cross-account role trust must require ExternalId
items.description: Cross-account AssumeRole trust without sts:ExternalId increases confused-deputy risk and third-party abuse paths.
items.remediation: Add sts:ExternalId condition for third-party cross-account trust relationships and rotate ExternalId values through change control.

pci_dss.reason: Context-bound access controls reduce role assumption abuse and authorization bypass risks.

items.title: IAM policies should not broadly allow identity provider mutation
items.description: Permissions to update SAML/OIDC providers can allow federation takeover and role impersonation if granted broadly.
items.remediation: Restrict IdP mutation actions to break-glass roles, add approvals, and monitor changes to SAML/OIDC provider configuration.

pci_dss.reason: High-impact federation administration must be strictly limited to authorized roles with explicit business justification.

items.title: IAM policies should not allow policy version escalation paths
items.description: CreatePolicyVersion/SetDefaultPolicyVersion can backdoor permissions and escalate access while appearing benign in current policy views.
items.remediation: Disallow policy-version mutation actions for non-security-admin roles and monitor CloudTrail for policy version creation/default switches.

pci_dss.reason: Policy version mutation can bypass least-privilege boundaries and must be tightly controlled.

items.title: IAM policies should not allow broad service-specific credential takeover
items.description: CreateServiceSpecificCredential and ResetServiceSpecificCredential over broad resources can be abused for persistence and lateral movement through service credentials (e.g., CodeCommit).
items.remediation: Limit service-specific credential actions to tightly scoped break-glass identities and monitor creation/reset events in CloudTrail.

pci_dss.reason: Credential issuance operations must be constrained to least privilege to prevent unauthorized access expansion.

items.title: IAM policies should not allow broad MFA device manipulation
items.description: EnableMFADevice, CreateVirtualMFADevice, DeactivateMFADevice, and ResyncMFADevice can be abused to lock out users or hijack MFA flows when granted broadly.
items.remediation: Restrict MFA lifecycle actions to limited security admin roles and alert on MFA device enrollment/deactivation events.

pci_dss.reason: MFA control integrity is critical; unauthorized MFA device operations can subvert authentication protections.

items.title: IAM wildcard delete permissions (iam:Delete*) must be prohibited
items.description: iam:Delete* grants a destructive blast radius over identities, policies, keys, and federation objects, enabling denial of service and anti-forensics.
items.remediation: Remove wildcard delete privileges, split destructive IAM actions into controlled emergency roles, and enforce approval workflows.

pci_dss.reason: Destructive identity and authorization actions must be granted only to explicitly authorized personnel with defined responsibilities.

items.title: IAM policies should not allow broad detachment/deletion of authorization controls
items.description: Detach* and DeletePolicyVersion/Delete*Policy actions over broad scope can remove guardrails and silently strip access controls for persistence or disruption.
items.remediation: Restrict policy detachment/deletion actions, require change approvals, and continuously monitor authorization-control modifications.

pci_dss.reason: Authorization-control changes must follow controlled and auditable change management to prevent unauthorized security regression.

notes: Expanded checklist covers CIS AWS Foundations v1.5.0 + AWS Security Best Practices. Includes critical, high, medium, and low severity items. Mapped to PCI DSS v4.0 controls.
